verdict.evidenceQuote: permission-modes (current): "With Claude Code v2.1.283 or later, auto mode is the built-in starting permission mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions." / "By default, classifier requests go to Claude Sonnet 5. If `/status` shows `Auto mode server` as `Enabled`, they're sent only for calls outside the server's review." Engineering post (dated Mar 25, 2026, no update note): "the transcript classifier (running on Sonnet 4.6)" ... "The 17% false-negative rate on real overeager actions is the honest number."
verdict.reason: I tried to defend the lesson and couldn't. In context, the callout's first sentence says auto mode has been the default for interactive sessions since v2.1.283. The next sentence uses 「その分類器」, so it reads as the classifier behind today's default auto mode. The only source for 17% is the engineering post. That post is dated Mar 25, 2026 and has no update note. Its number measures the full two-stage pipeline running on Sonnet 4.6, on 52 real overeager actions. Today's docs say classifier requests go to Sonnet 5 by default, or are reviewed on the server when that is enabled. So the lesson ties a figure from an older pipeline to the current classifier. That claims more than any page supports. The past tense 「見逃しました」 and the phrase 「Anthropicの検証で」 make the sentence sound historical, but the demonstrative still links the number to today's classifier. The lesson's broader point is still supported: the docs say "Auto mode reduces permission prompts but does not guarantee safety." Only the link between the number and the current classifier is wrong. The proposed fix is accurate. It dates the figure to the March 2026 official post and drops 「その」. It stays within the 60-character sentence budget and uses です・ます. No better fix is needed.

A `-p` session shows no workspace trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt." verdict.reason: I tried to defend the lesson. The case for it: "や" lists examples rather than everything, and some settings do apply in -p (the env block and helpers like apiKeyHelper are "Used"). Even so, the plain phrase "リポジトリの…設定が動きます" claims more than the docs say. The permissions page says the trust-gated settings, permissions.allow and additionalDirectories, are "Not used" under -p. Its table also marks subagent-frontmatter hooks and extraKnownMarketplaces as "Not used". The context makes the misreading likely. The block right before it (s2-defs) defines workspace trust as the check that keeps a project's allow rules from applying until you approve. The next sentence then says that in -p, where no check appears, the repository's "設定" run without confirmation. A learner would conclude that -p skips the trust gate, so allow rules apply too. The docs say the opposite. When the headless page lists what -p runs without trust, it names only two things: hooks in .claude/settings.json and .mcp.json servers. The proposed fix uses exactly those two items, so it is accurate and needs no betterFix. The sentence is about 50 chars, under the 60-char budget. It puts spaces around inline code, which matches the lesson's existing style. verdict.evidenceQuote: "Claude Code shows the trust dialog in interactive sessions only. A `claude -p` run or an SDK session never shows it, and trusting a parent folder doesn't count for these rules" ... table, `claude -p` column: "Hooks in settings files, the env block and helper commands such as apiKeyHelper, and a project skill's hooks and allowed-tools | ... | Used" / "`permissions.allow` rules and `additionalDirectories` in `.claude/settings.json` | Not used until you accept the trust dialog, which appears again listing them | Not used. Claude Code prints a `this workspace has not been trusted` warning to stderr" / "Frontmatter hooks in a project subagent, a project @skills-dir plugin, and extraKnownMarketplaces entries ... | Not used" / "Servers in `.mcp.json`, including ones the repository approves in its own settings | ... | Connected without asking, approved or not." Also https://code.claude.com/docs/en/security: "Note: A `-p` session shows neither prompt."
verdict.reason:
Part of the lesson is right. The docs confirm that `-p` shows no trust dialog ("A -p session shows neither prompt"). They also confirm that hooks in settings files, the `env` block and helpers such as `apiKeyHelper` are used in a `-p` run, and those last two are settings. So the sentence is not plain false.

The problem is the bare word 設定 ("settings"). The permissions page splits the repository's settings into two groups. The capability-granting ones that the trust dialog exists to gate, `permissions.allow` and `additionalDirectories`, are explicitly "Not used" in `-p`, and Claude Code warns "this workspace has not been trusted". Subagent frontmatter hooks, `@skills-dir` plugins and `extraKnownMarketplaces` are not used either.

Context makes the wording worse. Option d's feedback in the same question defines the trust dialog as the screen where you decide whether to turn on that folder's settings (そのフォルダーの設定を有効にするか). Read next to it, "-p uses the repository's settings without the dialog" tells the learner that `-p` acts as if the folder were trusted. The page says the opposite for exactly the settings the dialog gates. So the lesson says more than the page supports.

The proposed fix holds up. It keeps "hooks" (settings-file hooks: "Used") and swaps 設定 for `.mcp.json` servers ("Connected without asking, approved or not."). That item is precisely supported and is the bigger risk: `-p` also skips the separate `.mcp.json` approval prompt. The rest of the sentence is unchanged and the spacing around inline code is fine, so no betterFix is needed.

verdict.evidenceQuote: "Read and Edit deny rules apply to Claude's built-in file tools, to file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, such as `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, and `tee`, and to the targets of Bash redirections such as `> file` and `< file`. They don't apply to a command that reads files without naming them, such as `grep -r pattern .` run from the directory that holds the file, or to arbitrary subprocesses that read or write files indirectly, like a Python or Node script that opens files itself. For OS-level enforcement that blocks all processes from accessing a path, enable the sandbox." (The settings-reference permissions.deny entry says the same: Claude Code "excludes matching files from file discovery and search results, denies reads of them ... they don't apply to a command that reads files without naming them, such as `grep -r pattern .`, or to arbitrary subprocesses".)
verdict.reason: The finding stands. In the lesson, step ex-verify tells the learner to check `/permissions` and then ask Claude to read the file. The expected result it gives is the absolute "Claudeは中身を読めません。" The best support I found is in settings-reference: Claude Code "denies reads of them" and leaves the matching files out of discovery and search results. That backs a refused read through Claude's file tools. It does not back "Claude cannot read the contents." Both the permissions page and settings-reference say the deny rules only cover the built-in file tools, the Bash file commands Claude Code recognizes (cat, head, tail, sed, tee) and redirection targets. They do not cover `grep -r pattern .` run from the folder that holds the file, or scripts that open files themselves. grep is also a read-only command, which can run without asking, so Claude could see the contents that way. The s3-pitfall callout that follows does mention the script gap. It does not mention grep -r, and the expect line still promises more than the docs do. The proposed fix "Readツールや `cat` での読み取りが拒否されます。" matches the documented scope: built-in file tools and recognized commands such as cat are denied. It uses です・ます and fits the spacing style used elsewhere in the lesson, so no betterFix is needed.

verdict.evidenceQuote: On Linux and macOS, Claude Code refuses to start in `bypassPermissions` mode when running as root or under `sudo`: ... --dangerously-skip-permissions cannot be used with root/sudo privileges for security reasons ... The check is skipped automatically inside a recognized sandbox. To run autonomously in a container, use the dev container configuration, which runs Claude Code as a non-root user.
verdict.reason: I fetched the official permission-modes page, and the core fact is real: Claude Code refuses to start in bypassPermissions as root or under sudo. But the page gives two limits. The check applies on Linux and macOS only, and it is skipped inside a recognized sandbox. The lesson's feedback for e2 option d says 'Claude Codeは、rootやsudoでの `bypassPermissions` を拒否します。' with no OS scope and no exception, so it states the rule as universal, which is stronger than the page. Searching the current CHANGELOG for root and sudo turned up no entry that widens the check. The proposed fix closely translates the page's main sentence ('On Linux and macOS, Claude Code refuses to start in bypassPermissions mode when running as root or under sudo'). It also changes '拒否' to '起動を拒否', which matches 'refuses to start'. The fix leaves out the recognized-sandbox exception, but option d is about starting with sudo on an ordinary machine, where that exception does not apply. Adding 'サンドボックス' there could also be confused with the Bash /sandbox feature from option c. The fix is about 56 characters, inside the 60-character sentence budget. So the finding stands and the proposed fix is acceptable as written.

verdict.evidenceQuote: "The table below shows what Claude can do without a permission prompt in each mode." ... "| `bypassPermissions` | Everything | Isolated containers and VMs only |" and "`bypassPermissions` mode disables permission prompts and safety checks so tool calls execute immediately, including writes to protected paths."
verdict.reason: The lesson cell is a summary row in a three-column table (場面 / 起きうること / 合う対策), and the block cites cc-permission-modes. That page's own summary table puts bypassPermissions under "What runs without asking" with the value "Everything". So 「確認なしで何でも動く」 is a faithful translation of the official summary cell, not something stronger. The row's third column, 「ネットにつながらないコンテナやVMだけで使う」, matches the same table's "Isolated containers and VMs only". The page also says "disables permission prompts and safety checks so tool calls execute immediately". The exceptions the auditor quotes (deny rules still block; explicit ask rules, critical-path rm/rmdir and a few other actions still prompt) are real, but they are details in the page body. The official page itself does not repeat them in its summary table. Inside the lesson, the glossary entry 「拒否ルール…どの権限モードでも効きます」 and the q-feedback about deny rules already cover the deny-rule point, so a learner is not left with a wrong model. The proposed fix is also weaker than the original. 「拒否ルール以外は、ほぼ確認なしで動く」 suggests that deny rules make an action prompt when they actually block it outright. It also leaves out ask rules and critical-path removals, which still prompt. And it softens a risk warning the official page itself states bluntly ("offers no protection against prompt injection or unintended actions"). No change is needed.
